summary.text: 月 is interpreted as a pictograph of a half moon. A reported paleographic analysis says 月 and 夕 once shared a moon-shaped graph before later graphic specialization; Shang inscriptions attest 月 for both the moon and a calendar month, though the order of those uses is unresolved.

formation.text: The whole graph depicts a half moon; the evidence identifies no smaller semantic or phonetic components. Early forms are described as moon pictures. Bronze forms continue that graphic line, while the small-seal form is reported to have changed; the precise change is not established here.

components.text: The whole graph 月 is a pictorial depiction of a half moon. Treat it as one indivisible picture, not as a combination of smaller components.

history.text: The selected oracle-script image is a modern rendering linked to a specific Sinica record; the selected seal-script image is a modern reconstruction of the Shuowen tradition. They compare graphic forms but do not establish a precise sequence or first attestation.

A reported paleographic analysis says 月 and 夕 once shared a moon-shaped graph; an interior dot did not initially distinguish them. It reports later graphic specialization associating the dotted form with 月 and the undotted form with 夕. The date and mechanism of this differentiation remain unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The cited sources report Shang uses for both the moon and calendar months but do not establish which use came first or the character’s precise first dated attestation.
Proposed word-family and cognate explanations are not assessed here, and no particular proposal is endorsed.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone period; precise dating unresolved
senses.text: 月 is used for the moon in current Chinese, and Shang oracle-bone examples attest the same use, including in an eclipse context. These are early examples, but the precise first dated occurrence is not established here.

The current Chinese dictionary records 月 with the meaning ‘each month’. Shang inscriptions also attest its use for a calendar month, associated with the moon’s waxing and waning cycle; the chronology relative to the moon sense is unresolved, and these examples do not establish the sense’s first occurrence.

developments.text: The calendar-month sense is explained through the moon’s recurring waxing and waning. Since both uses are reported in Shang material, this explanation does not establish a chronological transition.

limitations.text: Later dictionary senses are recorded, but their first occurrences and semantic transitions are not detailed here.
Supplied readings concern 月 as a whole; no component-to-character sound comparison applies because no phonetic component is proposed.

overview.text: 月 is interpreted as a picture of a half moon and is the current Chinese word for “moon.” A reported analysis says it shared an early graph with 夕 before the forms became distinct.

components.text: This is the complete half-moon picture, not a combination of smaller parts.

items.period: Shang oracle-bone script; source record is identified as 簠天1, 合33694, 歷組
items.caption: This oracle-script form has a long central stroke and a curved outer stroke that frame a crescent-shaped opening, a shape consistent with 月 as a moon pictograph.
items.alt: Black glyph with a long vertical stroke beside a curved outer stroke, leaving a crescent-shaped opening.
items.selection_reason: The visible strokes match the documented half-moon pictographic account. The form is identified with a specific Shang oracle-bone record.

items.period: Shuowen small-seal script tradition; the image is a modern vector reconstruction
items.caption: This small-seal form has a rounded enclosing outline, an interior cross-stroke, and a curved extension below.
items.alt: Black rounded glyph with an oval outline, a short interior stroke, a cross-stroke, and a long curved lower extension.
items.selection_reason: It offers a useful graphic comparison: the rounded, less crescent-like outline shows how a later script tradition rendered 月. It is a modern reconstruction of the Shuowen seal-script tradition.

limitations.text: Both images are modern redrawings rather than photographs of ancient inscriptions. The oracle form is linked to a specific record, but the precise date of that inscription and the character’s first dated attestation are not established here.
